entry.title: Installing Gentoo • New to Gentoo, installing on an old office PC, where do I start with partitioning?
entry.content:
Hi everyone, I am Member and I am new here. I have an old office PC that runs Windows very slowly now, and I would like to try Gentoo on it for basic daily work, browser, documents and email, nothing fancy.

I have booted the Gentoo Live GUI and started reading the handbook, but I am stuck at the partitioning step. I am not sure whether to keep Windows as a dual boot or wipe the disk completely, and I do not want to lose the files already on the PC.

A few beginner questions:

For a simple desktop setup, is dual boot worth the extra trouble, or is it easier for a first install to use the whole disk?
How do I know if my PC is UEFI or BIOS, and does that change what I should choose for partitioning?
For a basic desktop, which stage3 and profile should I start with, so I do not pick something meant for a server?
I have backed up the important files already, I just do not want to make a basic mistake at the start. Any simple guidance for a first-time installer would be really helpful. Thanks in advance.

entry.title: Installing Gentoo • Can no longer shutdown
entry.content:
[This is not an "Installing" issue, but it's not the kernel either. Not sure where to post.]

"reboot", "shutdown now" and "shutdown -hp now" used to reboot, drop to single-user mode and poweroff, respectively. Now all three stop short of the end goal. They stop all services, then hang. The last message is "Deactivating swap devices ...". Workaround is count to ten, then press and hold the power button to poweroff. No apparent damage, the filesystems are clean when powering back on.

I should have jumped on it when it first happened a few months ago, now it's a little late. It doesn't seem to be a kernel panic, there is nothing in /sys/fs/pstore. I tried old kernels from backups, all the way back to 6.6.62 (2024, definitely worked then) but no difference. So it's not the kernel.

openrc? sysvinit? I can't easily downgrade either one, the earlier versions dropped out of ::gentoo. Not sure where else to look.

Any ideas? Here's emerge --info.

entry.title: Installing Gentoo • Upgrading to gcc16 *during* install - emerge --emptytree a good idea?
entry.content:
Hi, I've got a rather convoluted install, which takes over a day of continuous work to get it booted. One of the (many side quest) activities I perform is tupgrading from gcc 15 to gcc16 during the install.

Previous installs I always performed an emerge --emptytree --usepkg=n @system (and during some installation attempts, @world instead).

Is there a way to do this but skip all binary packages that are installed? I have my make.conf set to install binary packages system-wide by default, so the vast majority of my system is x64 v3 binary packages, and performing an emptytree re-install of Gentoo pre-built binaries seems like a waste of time (and bandwidth, to boot). Of course, if there is a reason I should reinstall all the installed binaries too, I'd like to know.

Also, a separate question:

Also, in my trials and tribulations over the last year with Gentoo installs, I've learned that (the currently available builds of) one particular app, wget2, does not like gcc16 at all - previously, version 2.2.0 was available to install, and it installed with gcc16 enabled just fine, though there was a bug report in that build that had a different issue. but both 2.2.1 and 2.3.0 fail to build on gcc16. My work-around this time during installation was to simply emerge 2.3.0 before upgrading to gcc16, since it seems to work just fine after building. As such, I currently have both gcc15 and gcc16 installed, gcc16 set to enabled, so I can quickly swap to 15 if a new release of wget2 drops that still has issues with gcc16. But will this cause me any problems in the long run?

entry.title: Installing Gentoo • Help for boot looping on first ever reboot
entry.content:
Hiya, I've just worked my way through the Gentoo Handbook and started the system for the first time.

I also followed the handbook on using LUKS.

When I boot the system, I'm prompted by my BIOS to enter the admin password. Then I'm prompted to decrypt my LUKS volume. These I do successfully.

I am then shown a fullscreen Gentoo logo with an option for UEFI boot options and a short countdown to boot.

When the timer expires, the system reboots and I'm back to the beginning.

I'm currently running my system off my live USB. It's an aged HP Pavilion 15 laptop that, until recently, ran Windows 10.

I would greatly appreciate any assistance in getting my system to boot. I'm a Gentoo and forum newbie so I apologise if I broke any etiquette with this post and will do better next time.

Thank you.

entry.title: Installing Gentoo • Questions about /etc/fstab and UUID
entry.content:
I installed Gentoo for the first time now, following the handbook to the letter and I believe it to have been with initramfs(if that matters). I eventually had a look at /etc/fstab and was dumbfounded that it was all commented out and even some boot-time terminal message mentioned blank fstab. How can Gentoo function without it and am I going to run into some conflicts if I use one? I uncommented my root partition while adding new entries and it was mounted read-only next time. What baffles me the most that my / partition (sdd3) has one UUID (which we are supposed to rely on rather then /dev) in the auto-generated fstab and completely different one in output of lsblk -o - that makes a sham out of the "unique id" concept. Also, which one is true?
